skills.mechanism: Explain with a mechanism, not a restatement
skills.data: Describe data with values, units and the comparison
skills.design: Variables, controls and what a control rules out
skills.prediction: Predict a result and justify it with a mechanism
skills.argument: Support or refute a claim with evidence and reasoning
skills.models: Use a model or diagram to explain a process
skills.stats: Error bars, variation and whether a difference is meaningful

prompts.title: Why water warms more slowly than oil
prompts.context: A student heats 500 g of water and 500 g of vegetable oil on identical hot plates. Each sample absorbs 21,000 J of energy. The water warms from 20.0 °C to 30.0 °C. The oil warms from 20.0 °C to about 41 °C.
prompts.prompt: Explain, at the level of molecules, why the same amount of energy raised the temperature of the water less than the temperature of the oil.
checklist: Says water molecules are polar and form hydrogen bonds with each other, while oil molecules are nonpolar and do not
Says part of the energy absorbed by the water breaks hydrogen bonds instead of making the molecules move faster
Links temperature to the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so less energy going into motion means a smaller temperature rise

earns.answer: Water molecules are polar. The partial negative oxygen of one water molecule is attracted to the partial positive hydrogens of its neighbors, so the molecules are held together by many hydrogen bonds. Oil molecules are nonpolar and form no hydrogen bonds. When the water absorbed 21,000 J, part of that energy broke hydrogen bonds, and only the rest made the molecules move faster. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so the water warmed by 10 °C while the oil warmed by about 21 °C. This is why water has a high specific heat.
earns.why: It names the cause (hydrogen bonds between polar water molecules), says where the extra energy goes, and connects that to temperature as molecular motion.

misses.answer: Water has a higher specific heat than oil, so it takes more energy to heat up water.
misses.why: It restates the result with a name. It never says what in water's structure causes the high specific heat or where the absorbed energy goes.

prompts.title: Double bonds and melting point
prompts.context:
A student asks whether the number of double bonds in a fatty acid changes its melting point. The student measures the melting points of four pure fatty acids, three trials each, in a temperature-controlled bath. All four fatty acids have 18 carbons.

Fatty acidC=C double bondsMean melting point (°C)
Stearic acid069
Oleic acid113
Linoleic acid2−5
Linolenic acid3−11
prompts.prompt: Identify the independent and dependent variables, and explain why the student chose fatty acids that all have 18 carbons.
checklist: Independent variable: the number of C=C double bonds in the fatty acid (0, 1, 2 or 3)
Dependent variable: the melting point of the fatty acid, measured in °C
Says chain length also affects melting point, because longer chains have more contact and more attractions between neighboring chains
Says holding chain length constant lets the drop in melting point be linked to the double bonds and not to a difference in length

earns.answer: The independent variable is the number of C=C double bonds in each fatty acid: 0, 1, 2 or 3. The dependent variable is the melting point in °C. All four fatty acids have 18 carbons because chain length also changes melting point. Longer chains touch along more of their length, so more attractions form between neighboring chains. With chain length held constant, the drop in melting point from 69 °C to −11 °C can be linked to the double bonds and not to a difference in chain length.
earns.why: It names each variable precisely, with its values or units, and says which other explanation the constant chain length rules out.

misses.answer: The independent variable is the fatty acids and the dependent variable is temperature. The carbons are kept the same to make it a fair test.
misses.why: "The fatty acids" is not the factor that was changed, and "temperature" is vague: the measured outcome is each fatty acid's melting point, not the bath temperature. "Fair test" does not say what other cause is ruled out.

prompts.title: G-C content and DNA melting temperature
prompts.context:
Researchers heat four double-stranded DNA samples, each 500 base pairs long. For each sample they record the melting temperature: the temperature at which half of the DNA has separated into single strands.

G-C base pairs (% of all pairs)Melting temperature (°C)
3081.6
4085.7
5089.8
6093.9
prompts.prompt: Describe the relationship between G-C content and melting temperature, using values from the table, and explain it in terms of base pairing.
checklist: States the direction: as the percent of G-C pairs increases, the melting temperature increases
Cites values with units, such as 81.6 °C at 30% G-C and 93.9 °C at 60% G-C
Gives the size of the change: about 4.1 °C higher for every 10 percentage points of G-C, a steady rise
Explains that a G-C pair has three hydrogen bonds and an A-T pair has two, so more energy is needed to separate the strands

earns.answer: Melting temperature increases as G-C content increases. The sample with 30% G-C pairs melts at 81.6 °C and the sample with 60% G-C pairs melts at 93.9 °C, a rise of 12.3 °C. The rise is steady, about 4.1 °C for every 10 percentage points of G-C. A G-C pair is held together by three hydrogen bonds, while an A-T pair is held by two. DNA with more G-C pairs has more hydrogen bonds between its strands, so more energy, and a higher temperature, is needed to separate them.
earns.why: It gives the direction, real values with units and the size of the change, then explains the pattern with the number of hydrogen bonds per pair.

misses.answer: Higher G-C content makes DNA melt at a higher temperature because G-C pairs are stronger.
misses.why: The direction is right, but there are no values, units or size of change, and "stronger" is not explained with hydrogen bonds.

prompts.title: A charged R group inside a protein
prompts.context: A small protein folds into a compact shape with a pocket that binds a sugar molecule. Amino acid 42 sits in the protein's interior. Its R group is valine, which is nonpolar, and the R groups around it are also nonpolar. A lab makes a version of the protein that is identical except that amino acid 42 is aspartic acid, whose R group carries a negative charge at pH 7.
prompts.prompt: Predict how this change affects the protein's ability to bind the sugar, and justify your prediction.
checklist: Predicts that the changed protein binds the sugar less well or not at all
Says the charged R group is hydrophilic and is not stable buried among nonpolar R groups, so the hydrophobic interactions in the interior are disrupted
Says the protein folds differently, so its tertiary structure and the shape of the binding pocket change
Links the changed shape of the pocket to weaker binding: structure determines function

earns.answer: The changed protein will bind the sugar less well, or not at all. Tertiary structure depends on interactions between R groups. In the original protein, nonpolar valine is packed with other nonpolar R groups away from water, and these hydrophobic interactions hold the interior together. The negatively charged R group of aspartic acid is hydrophilic, so it is not stable buried among nonpolar R groups. The chain folds differently, which moves the charge toward water and changes the tertiary structure. The binding pocket changes shape, so the sugar fits less well and binding drops.
earns.why: It makes a clear prediction and justifies it with a chain of causes: R group polarity, then folding, then pocket shape, then function.

misses.answer: The protein will not work because an amino acid changed, and changing the amino acids changes the protein.
misses.why: It predicts without a mechanism. It says nothing about the polarity of the two R groups, how folding changes or why the pocket's shape matters.

prompts.title: A cube model of cell size
prompts.context:
A student models cells as cubes. Every µm³ of cytoplasm uses oxygen at the same rate, and oxygen can enter only across the surface.

Side length (µm)Surface area (µm²)Volume (µm³)Surface area ÷ volume (per µm)
106001,0000.60
202,4008,0000.30
409,60064,0000.15
prompts.prompt: Use the model to explain why the size of a cell is limited.
checklist: Uses values: doubling the side multiplies surface area by 4 but volume by 8, so the ratio halves (0.60 to 0.30 per µm)
Says surface area sets the rate of exchange, because materials enter and leave only across the plasma membrane
Says volume sets how much material the cell uses, so demand grows faster than supply as the cell grows
Concludes that above some size, exchange across the surface is too slow to supply the whole volume

earns.answer: In the model, doubling the side from 10 µm to 20 µm multiplies the surface area by 4, from 600 to 2,400 µm², but the volume by 8, from 1,000 to 8,000 µm³. The surface area to volume ratio halves, from 0.60 to 0.30 per µm. Oxygen enters and wastes leave only across the plasma membrane, so surface area sets the rate of exchange. Volume sets how much oxygen the cell uses. As the cube grows, each µm³ of cytoplasm is served by less membrane. Above some size, exchange across the surface is too slow to supply the whole volume, so cell size is limited.
earns.why: It reads the model with numbers, says what surface area and volume each stand for, and uses the falling ratio to explain the limit.

misses.answer: Bigger cells have less surface area, so they cannot take in enough oxygen.
misses.why: A bigger cube has more surface area, not less. The limit comes from the ratio of surface area to volume, and the answer uses no values from the model.

prompts.title: Heated beet cells and a leaking red compound
prompts.context:
A red compound is stored inside beet cells and leaks out only through damaged membranes. Students held beet cubes at one temperature for 10 minutes, then placed each cube in room-temperature water for 30 minutes. They measured the absorbance of the water: more of the red compound gives a higher absorbance. Each mean is from 5 cubes, and the ± value gives the 95% confidence interval (mean ± 2 SE).

Temperature (°C)Mean absorbance ± 2 SE
250.12 ± 0.03
400.15 ± 0.04
550.48 ± 0.06
700.91 ± 0.07
prompts.prompt: A student says that heating from 25 °C to 40 °C damaged the membranes. Evaluate the claim using the confidence intervals, and compare it with the change from 40 °C to 55 °C.
checklist: Gives the intervals at 25 °C (0.09 to 0.15) and 40 °C (0.11 to 0.19) and notes that they overlap
Concludes the 25 °C to 40 °C difference is not good evidence of damage: it could come from variation between cubes
Shows the intervals at 40 °C (0.11 to 0.19) and 55 °C (0.42 to 0.54) do not overlap, so that increase is likely real

earns.answer: The data do not support the claim. The 95% confidence interval at 25 °C runs from 0.09 to 0.15, and at 40 °C it runs from 0.11 to 0.19. The intervals overlap a lot, so the rise in mean absorbance from 0.12 to 0.15 may come from variation between cubes, not from membrane damage. From 40 °C to 55 °C the mean rises from 0.15 to 0.48, and the intervals, 0.11 to 0.19 and 0.42 to 0.54, do not overlap. That increase is very likely real, so the evidence points to membrane damage starting between 40 °C and 55 °C.
earns.why: It turns each mean ± 2 SE into an interval, uses overlap to judge each difference, and reaches a conclusion that matches the evidence.

misses.answer: The claim is supported because absorbance went up from 0.12 to 0.15, so more of the red compound leaked at 40 °C.
misses.why: It compares only the means. With overlapping 95% confidence intervals, a difference this small is not good evidence of a real change.

prompts.title: What each control rules out
prompts.context:
Researchers make small artificial vesicles from a phospholipid bilayer. In some, they insert aquaporin, a channel protein for water. They place vesicles in a solution and measure the percent increase in vesicle volume after 10 s.

GroupAquaporin in vesicleOutside solutionMean volume increase after 10 s (%)
AYesHypotonic28
BNoHypotonic3
CYesIsotonic0
prompts.prompt: Identify the independent and dependent variables for groups A and B, and explain what group B and group C each rule out.
checklist: Independent variable: whether aquaporin is in the vesicle membrane
Dependent variable: percent increase in vesicle volume after 10 s
Group B shows how much water crosses the bare bilayer (3%), ruling out the bilayer alone as the cause of the fast swelling in group A
Group C rules out the protein itself or the handling of the vesicles as a cause of swelling, since without a concentration difference there is no net water entry

earns.answer: The independent variable is whether aquaporin is in the vesicle membrane. The dependent variable is the percent increase in vesicle volume after 10 s. Group B has no aquaporin but is in the same hypotonic solution, and its vesicles swell only 3%. Water crosses the bare bilayer slowly, so the bilayer alone does not explain the 28% swelling in group A. The faster water entry is due to aquaporin. Group C has aquaporin but is in an isotonic solution, and its volume does not change. This rules out the idea that inserting the protein or handling the vesicles causes swelling by itself. Net water movement needs a difference in solute concentration across the membrane.
earns.why: It names both variables with their measurement and says, for each control, which other explanation it removes.

misses.answer: The independent variable is aquaporin and the dependent variable is swelling. Groups B and C are the controls, so the results can be compared.
misses.why: It calls B and C controls without saying what each one rules out, and the dependent variable has no measurement or time.

prompts.title: Potato cores in sucrose solutions
prompts.context:
Students placed potato cores in sucrose solutions at 22 °C and measured each core's mass before and after 24 hours. Each value is the mean of 4 cores.

Sucrose (M)Mean change in mass (%)
0.0+18.5
0.2+6.1
0.4−4.2
0.6−12.8
0.8−17.0
prompts.prompt: Describe the effect of sucrose concentration on the change in mass, using values from the table, estimate the sucrose concentration at which there is no net movement of water, and explain the gain and loss of mass in terms of water potential.
checklist: States the direction with values: from a gain of 18.5% in 0.0 M to a loss of 17.0% in 0.8 M sucrose
Notes the change in mass crosses zero between 0.2 M (+6.1%) and 0.4 M (−4.2%)
Estimates about 0.32 M (any value near 0.3 M) as the concentration with no net water movement
Explains gain and loss with water potential: water moves from the higher to the lower water potential

earns.answer: As sucrose concentration increases, the cores gain less mass and then lose mass. In 0.0 M the cores gained 18.5% of their mass, and in 0.8 M they lost 17.0%. The change crosses zero between 0.2 M (+6.1%) and 0.4 M (−4.2%). Reading between those points, the change in mass is zero at about 0.32 M. There the water potential of the solution equals that of the potato cells, so there is no net water movement. In weaker solutions the solution has the higher water potential and water moves into the cells; in stronger ones water moves out.
earns.why: It describes the trend with values and units, locates the zero crossing from two data points and explains both sides with water potential.

misses.answer: The more sucrose, the more mass the potato cores lost. The cores are isotonic at about 0.4 M.
misses.why: It gives no values, misses that cores gained mass in weak solutions, and ignores that cores already lost 4.2% at 0.4 M.

prompts.title: A saliva enzyme at stomach pH
prompts.context:
Amylase from saliva breaks starch into smaller sugars. Students measured its activity at 37 °C at several pH values, as a percent of its highest activity.

pHActivity (% of maximum)
415
548
692
7100
871
prompts.prompt: Predict the rate of starch breakdown by this enzyme at pH 2, and justify your prediction with a mechanism.
checklist: Predicts activity near zero at pH 2, lower than the 15% measured at pH 4
Uses the trend: activity falls from 100% at pH 7 to 15% at pH 4 as pH drops
Says the high H+ concentration changes the charges on R groups, breaking ionic and hydrogen bonds that hold the enzyme's shape
Says the active site changes shape, so starch fits poorly and few enzyme-substrate complexes form

earns.answer: The rate at pH 2 will be close to zero, lower than the 15% measured at pH 4. Activity drops steadily as pH falls below 7: 92% at pH 6, 48% at pH 5 and 15% at pH 4. At pH 2 the H+ concentration is 100 times higher than at pH 4. The extra H+ ions bind to R groups that are normally negatively charged, which changes their charges. Ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds between R groups break, so the enzyme's tertiary structure and its active site change shape. Starch no longer fits the active site well, so few enzyme-substrate complexes form and little starch is broken down.
earns.why: The prediction follows the data, and the justification is a chain from H+ to R group charges to active site shape to rate.

misses.answer: The rate will be lower because the acid at pH 2 denatures the enzyme.
misses.why: The direction is right, but it uses no data and "denatures" names the outcome without saying how H+ changes R groups and the active site.

prompts.title: Where does inhibitor X bind?
prompts.context:
Researchers measured the rate of an enzyme reaction at four substrate concentrations, with and without a fixed amount of inhibitor X.

Substrate (mM)Rate, no inhibitor (µmol/min)Rate, with X (µmol/min)
1104
53016
204434
804947

A student claims that X binds to the enzyme's active site.
prompts.prompt: Support or refute the student's claim using evidence from the table and reasoning about how inhibitors work.
checklist: Supports the claim, citing low substrate evidence: at 1 mM the rate falls from 10 to 4 µmol/min with X, 60% lower
Cites high substrate evidence: at 80 mM the rate is 47 versus 49 µmol/min, only about 4% lower
Reasons that X and substrate compete for the active site, so at high substrate most active sites hold substrate and few bind X
Says an inhibitor that bound elsewhere and changed the enzyme's shape would still lower the rate at high substrate

earns.answer: The data support the claim. At 1 mM substrate, X lowers the rate from 10 to 4 µmol/min, a 60% drop. At 80 mM substrate, the rate with X is 47 µmol/min compared with 49 µmol/min without it, only about 4% lower. So adding more substrate almost cancels the effect of X. This fits a competitive inhibitor: X and the substrate compete for the same active site. At high substrate concentration, substrate molecules occupy most active sites, so X binds few enzymes. An inhibitor that bound somewhere else and changed the enzyme's shape would still lower the rate at high substrate, because extra substrate could not undo that change.
earns.why: It takes a side, uses values at both ends of the range, and explains why the pattern points to the active site and not to another site.

misses.answer: The claim is supported because X lowers the reaction rate at every substrate concentration.
misses.why: Any inhibitor lowers the rate. The evidence that matters is that high substrate almost removes the effect, and the answer gives no reasoning about competition.

prompts.title: Net oxygen output across light levels
prompts.context:
A student measured net oxygen production by a water plant at 25 °C under six light intensities. Net production is oxygen released by photosynthesis minus oxygen used by cellular respiration.

Light intensity (µmol photons/m²/s)Net O2 production (mL/h)
0−0.4
1000.8
2001.9
4003.2
8003.4
16003.4
prompts.prompt: Describe how net oxygen production changes with light intensity, using values from the table, and explain the value at 0 light and why production levels off at high light.
checklist: From 0 to 400 µmol photons/m²/s, net O2 production rises from −0.4 to 3.2 mL/h
Above 400, it levels off: 3.2 mL/h at 400 and 3.4 mL/h at both 800 and 1600
At 0 light the value is negative because the plant still uses O2 in cellular respiration while no photosynthesis occurs
Gives a reason for the leveling off: something other than light, such as CO2 supply or Calvin cycle enzymes, limits the rate

earns.answer: Net oxygen production rises with light intensity at first, then levels off. It goes from −0.4 mL/h at 0 light to 0.8 mL/h at 100, 1.9 mL/h at 200 and 3.2 mL/h at 400 µmol photons/m²/s. Above 400 it barely changes: 3.4 mL/h at both 800 and 1600. At high light, another factor such as the CO2 supply or the speed of the Calvin cycle limits the rate. At 0 light the value is negative because the plant still uses oxygen in cellular respiration, but no photosynthesis releases oxygen, so it takes up 0.4 mL of O2 each hour.
earns.why: It describes both parts of the curve with values and units, and explains the negative value with respiration and the plateau with another limit.

misses.answer: Oxygen production goes up as light intensity goes up, because more light means more photosynthesis.
misses.why: It gives no values, misses the plateau above 400 and does not explain why the value at 0 light is negative.

prompts.title: A leak in the inner membrane
prompts.context:
Model: in the inner mitochondrial membrane, electrons from NADH pass along the electron transport chain to O2. As electrons pass, chain proteins pump H+ from the matrix into the intermembrane space. H+ flows back into the matrix through ATP synthase, and this flow drives ATP synthesis.

A compound lets H+ cross the inner membrane directly. In isolated mitochondria, adding the compound raised O2 use from 2.0 to 3.6 nmol/min per mg protein, while ATP production fell from 5.0 to 0.8 nmol/min per mg protein.
prompts.prompt: Use the model to explain why the compound lowers ATP production even though the mitochondria keep using O2.
checklist: Says electron transport to O2 still runs, so O2 is still used as the final electron acceptor
Says H+ pumped into the intermembrane space returns through the compound instead of through ATP synthase, so the H+ gradient is smaller
Says ATP synthase makes ATP only when H+ flows through it, so less flow through ATP synthase means less ATP (5.0 down to 0.8)

earns.answer: In the model, electrons from NADH pass along the electron transport chain to O2, the final electron acceptor. As they pass, the chain pumps H+ from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building a high H+ concentration there. Normally H+ flows back through ATP synthase, and that flow drives ATP synthesis. The compound gives H+ another path across the inner membrane. Electron transport still runs, so O2 is still used, but most H+ returns through the compound instead of ATP synthase. The H+ gradient becomes smaller and less H+ flows through ATP synthase, so ATP production falls from 5.0 to 0.8 nmol/min per mg protein.
earns.why: It uses each step of the model to separate electron transport (which uses O2) from ATP synthesis (which needs H+ flow through ATP synthase).

misses.answer: The compound stops the electron transport chain, so less ATP is made.
misses.why: It contradicts the data, since O2 use continued. It misses that the compound lets H+ bypass ATP synthase.

prompts.title: Blocking the off switch for cAMP
prompts.context: In liver cells, epinephrine binds a G protein-coupled receptor. The activated G protein activates adenylyl cyclase, which makes cAMP from ATP. cAMP activates protein kinase A, which starts a phosphorylation cascade that activates the enzyme that breaks glycogen into glucose. The enzyme phosphodiesterase breaks down cAMP. A drug blocks phosphodiesterase.
prompts.prompt: Predict how treating liver cells with the drug affects glucose release after a short pulse of epinephrine, and justify your prediction.
checklist: Predicts more glucose release, or release that continues longer after epinephrine is gone
Says cAMP is not broken down, so cAMP stays high after the signal
Says high cAMP keeps protein kinase A active, so the cascade keeps activating the enzyme that breaks glycogen into glucose

earns.answer: The treated cells will release more glucose, and release will continue longer after the epinephrine pulse ends. Normally phosphodiesterase breaks down cAMP, which shuts the pathway off once epinephrine leaves the receptor. With phosphodiesterase blocked, the cAMP made during the pulse is not broken down, so cAMP stays high. cAMP keeps protein kinase A active, and the phosphorylation cascade keeps the glycogen-breaking enzyme active. More glycogen is broken into glucose over a longer time.
earns.why: It makes a clear prediction and traces the effect through the pathway: cAMP level, then protein kinase A, then the enzyme, then glucose.

misses.answer: The cells will release less glucose because the drug blocks an enzyme in the pathway.
misses.why: Phosphodiesterase turns the signal off. Blocking it keeps cAMP high, so the response gets stronger, not weaker.

prompts.title: Why insulin release is negative feedback
prompts.context: After a meal, a student's blood glucose rose from 90 mg/dL to 140 mg/dL. Cells in the pancreas released insulin. Insulin bound to receptors on liver and muscle cells, which took up glucose and stored it as glycogen. Within 2 hours blood glucose was back near 90 mg/dL, and insulin release had dropped.
prompts.prompt: Explain how these events make up a negative feedback loop.
checklist: Names the stimulus: the rise in blood glucose is detected by pancreas cells, which release insulin
Gives the response: insulin binding to liver and muscle cells leads to glucose uptake and storage as glycogen, so blood glucose falls
Says the response reduces the stimulus: as glucose returns toward 90 mg/dL, insulin release decreases
Says this is negative feedback because the response opposes the change, not because a level goes down

earns.answer: The stimulus is the rise in blood glucose from 90 to 140 mg/dL. Cells in the pancreas detect the higher glucose and release insulin. Insulin binds to receptors on liver and muscle cells, and these cells take up glucose and store it as glycogen. Blood glucose falls back toward 90 mg/dL. As glucose falls, the stimulus for the pancreas cells gets weaker, so insulin release drops. The response reduces the change that caused it, which returns glucose to its set level. That is negative feedback.
earns.why: It traces the full loop, stimulus to response and back, and defines negative feedback by the response opposing the change.

misses.answer: Insulin lowers blood sugar, which is negative feedback because it makes the glucose level go down.
misses.why: "Negative" does not mean the level goes down. It skips the loop: the falling glucose reducing insulin release.

prompts.title: A compound that changes phase counts
prompts.context:
Students counted 1,000 cells in onion root tips from a control group and from roots treated for 12 hours with a compound.

PhaseControl (cells)Treated (cells)
Interphase880790
Prophase7060
Metaphase20140
Anaphase155
Telophase155
prompts.prompt: Describe how the treatment changed the distribution of cells among the phases, using values from the table, and identify the step the compound most likely blocks.
checklist: Metaphase cells rise from 20 (2.0%) to 140 (14.0%), seven times as many
Anaphase plus telophase cells fall from 30 (3.0%) to 10 (1.0%)
Cells in mitosis rise from 120 (12.0%) to 210 (21.0%) of the 1,000 counted
Identifies the block: cells reach metaphase but do not move on to anaphase

earns.answer: The treatment raised the number of cells in metaphase from 20 to 140 of 1,000, or from 2.0% to 14.0%, seven times as many. Cells in anaphase and telophase together fell from 30 (3.0%) to 10 (1.0%). The share of cells in mitosis rose from 12.0% to 21.0%, while interphase cells fell from 880 to 790. Cells keep entering mitosis and reaching metaphase, but few move on to anaphase. The compound most likely blocks the step from metaphase to anaphase, so cells pile up in metaphase.
earns.why: It compares control and treated values for each relevant phase, with the size of each change, then draws a conclusion the numbers support.

misses.answer: The treated roots have more cells in metaphase, so the compound affects mitosis.
misses.why: It gives no values, misses the drop in anaphase and telophase, and does not name which step is blocked.

prompts.title: Does more growth factor help?
prompts.context:
Researchers grew cells for 24 hours with no growth factor, 10 ng/mL or 50 ng/mL of a growth factor, then measured the percent of cells that had entered S phase. Each mean is from 6 dishes; the ± value gives the 95% confidence interval (mean ± 2 SE).

Growth factor (ng/mL)Cells in S phase (%, mean ± 2 SE)
08 ± 3
1024 ± 4
5027 ± 5

A student claims that raising the dose from 10 to 50 ng/mL makes more cells pass the G1 checkpoint.
prompts.prompt: Evaluate the student's claim using the confidence intervals.
checklist: Gives the intervals at 10 ng/mL (20% to 28%) and 50 ng/mL (22% to 32%) and notes that they overlap
Concludes the claim is not supported: the 3 percentage point difference between means (24% and 27%) could come from variation between dishes
Contrasts with 0 versus 10 ng/mL: intervals of 5% to 11% and 20% to 28% do not overlap, so the growth factor itself does increase S phase entry

earns.answer: The claim is not supported. At 10 ng/mL the 95% confidence interval is 20% to 28%, and at 50 ng/mL it is 22% to 32%. These intervals overlap, so the difference between the means, 24% and 27%, may come from variation between dishes and is not good evidence of a real effect. The growth factor itself does matter: with none, the interval is 5% to 11%, which does not overlap the interval at 10 ng/mL. So adding growth factor makes more cells pass the G1 checkpoint, but these data show no clear extra effect from raising the dose to 50 ng/mL.
earns.why: It converts each mean ± 2 SE into an interval, judges both comparisons by overlap, and keeps the conclusion within what the data show.

misses.answer: The claim is supported because 27% of cells entered S phase at 50 ng/mL compared with 24% at 10 ng/mL.
misses.why: It compares means without the intervals. The intervals overlap, so this small difference is not good evidence of a real effect.

prompts.title: More than eight kinds of gametes
prompts.context: An animal has a diploid number of 2n = 6, so its cells hold three pairs of homologous chromosomes. In each pair, one chromosome came from its mother and one from its father, and the two carry different alleles of many genes. A student says this animal can make only 2³ = 8 genetically different kinds of gametes.
prompts.prompt: Explain how meiosis produces genetically different gametes in this animal, and why the number of kinds is much larger than 8.
checklist: Independent assortment: in metaphase I each homologous pair lines up independently of the others, giving 2³ = 8 combinations of whole chromosomes
Crossing over: in prophase I nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange segments, making chromosomes with new combinations of alleles
Says crossing over can happen at different places in each meiosis, so the gametes are not limited to the 8 combinations of whole chromosomes

earns.answer: In metaphase I, each pair of homologous chromosomes lines up at the middle of the cell independently of the other pairs. Which chromosome of a pair goes to which pole is random, so with three pairs there are 2³ = 8 combinations of whole maternal and paternal chromosomes. This is independent assortment. Earlier, in prophase I, nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange segments by crossing over. Each recombinant chromatid carries some maternal and some paternal alleles. Crossovers can occur at different places in each meiosis, so the chromosomes in gametes are new mixtures, and the number of kinds of gametes is far larger than 8.
earns.why: It names both sources of variation, places each in its stage of meiosis, and says why crossing over breaks the limit of 8.

misses.answer: Meiosis shuffles the chromosomes, and crossing over also happens, so there are more than 8 kinds.
misses.why: It names the processes but explains neither: how pairs line up in metaphase I or how crossing over makes new allele combinations.

prompts.title: Testing a 9:3:3:1 ratio
prompts.context:
In a plant, purple flowers (P) are dominant to white (p), and tall stems (T) are dominant to short (t). Two plants with genotype PpTt are crossed, giving 320 offspring.

PhenotypeObserved (plants)
Purple, tall172
Purple, short66
White, tall61
White, short21

The critical value for 3 degrees of freedom at p = 0.05 is 7.81.
prompts.prompt: Calculate the chi-square value and determine whether the data support the hypothesis that the two genes assort independently.
checklist: Expected counts from 9:3:3:1 of 320: 180, 60, 60 and 20 plants
Chi-square ≈ 1.02, with 3 degrees of freedom (4 classes minus 1)
Compares 1.02 with 7.81: fails to reject the null hypothesis, so the differences can be explained by chance and the data fit independent assortment

earns.answer: For independent assortment the null hypothesis predicts a 9:3:3:1 ratio. Of 320 plants, the expected counts are 180, 60, 60 and 20. Chi-square = (172 − 180)²/180 + (66 − 60)²/60 + (61 − 60)²/60 + (21 − 20)²/20 = 0.356 + 0.600 + 0.017 + 0.050 ≈ 1.02. There are 4 classes, so 3 degrees of freedom. Since 1.02 is less than the critical value 7.81, I fail to reject the null hypothesis. The differences between observed and expected counts are small enough to be explained by chance, so the data support independent assortment.
earns.why: It shows the expected counts, the calculation and the degrees of freedom, compares with the critical value and states what failing to reject means.

misses.answer: The observed numbers are not exactly 9:3:3:1, so the genes do not assort independently.
misses.why: Random chance always makes counts differ a little. Without a chi-square test, the answer cannot judge whether the difference is too large to be chance.

prompts.title: Are these genes on different chromosomes?
prompts.context:
In a beetle, shiny shell (S) is dominant to dull (s), and long antennae (L) are dominant to short (l). A female that inherited S and L from one parent and s and l from the other is crossed with a dull, short male (ssll). The cross gives 1,000 offspring.

PhenotypeOffspring
Shiny, long412
Dull, short418
Shiny, short87
Dull, long83

A student claims the two genes are on different chromosomes.
prompts.prompt: Support or refute the student's claim using the data and reasoning about how chromosomes are inherited.
checklist: Refutes the claim that the two genes are on different chromosomes
Says genes on different chromosomes would give about 250 of each class (1:1:1:1), but the parental classes are 412 and 418 and the new combinations only 87 and 83
Reasons that the genes are linked on one chromosome, so their alleles are inherited together unless crossing over occurs between them
Uses the recombinant offspring: 170 of 1,000, or 17%, come from crossing over between the two genes

earns.answer: The data refute the claim. If the genes were on different chromosomes, they would assort independently and the testcross would give about 250 offspring in each of the four classes. Instead, the two parental combinations, shiny long (412) and dull short (418), make up 830 of 1,000 offspring, while the new combinations total only 170. This means the genes are linked: S and L sit on one chromosome and s and l on its homolog, so they are usually inherited together. The 170 recombinant offspring, 17%, come from crossing over between the two genes during meiosis in the female.
earns.why: It compares the observed counts with what independent assortment predicts, and explains both the excess of parental types and the recombinants.

misses.answer: The claim is wrong because the four groups are not equal, so the genes must be linked.
misses.why: It gives no counts or expected values and does not explain why linked genes give mostly parental types or where the recombinants come from.

prompts.title: Temperature and flower color
prompts.context: Researchers took 40 cuttings from one parent plant and grew them into new plants. They grew 20 at 15 °C and 20 at 30 °C, with the same light, soil, pot size and watering. At 15 °C, 18 plants had red flowers and 2 had pink flowers. At 30 °C, 19 had white flowers and 1 had red flowers.
prompts.prompt: Identify the independent and dependent variables, explain why the researchers used cuttings from a single parent plant, and state what the results show about genotype and phenotype.
checklist: Independent variable: growing temperature (15 °C or 30 °C)
Dependent variable: flower color, counted as the number of plants with red, pink or white flowers
Says cuttings from one parent are genetically identical, so differences in genotype are ruled out as a cause of the color difference
Concludes the color difference is an effect of the environment on the phenotype, since light, soil and water were held constant

earns.answer: The independent variable is the growing temperature, 15 °C or 30 °C. The dependent variable is flower color, counted as the number of plants with each color. Cuttings from one parent plant are genetically identical, so all 40 plants have the same genotype. This rules out genetic differences as the cause of the color difference. Light, soil, pot size and watering were also the same. So the change from mostly red flowers at 15 °C (18 of 20) to mostly white flowers at 30 °C (19 of 20) shows that temperature changes the phenotype produced by one genotype.
earns.why: It names each variable and how it was measured, and says what the identical genotype rules out and what conclusion that allows.

misses.answer: The independent variable is the plants and the dependent variable is the color. Cuttings were used so the plants would be the same.
misses.why: The plants are not the variable that was changed, and "the same" does not say that genotype is the alternative cause being ruled out.

prompts.title: From codons to a short peptide
prompts.context: Model: an mRNA strand reads 5′ AUG GCU UGG AAA UAA 3′. A ribosome binds the mRNA. Each tRNA has a three-base anticodon at one end and carries one amino acid at the other. The genetic code gives AUG = methionine (Met), GCU = alanine (Ala), UGG = tryptophan (Trp), AAA = lysine (Lys) and UAA = stop. The ribosome makes the peptide Met-Ala-Trp-Lys.
prompts.prompt: Use the model to explain how the base sequence of this mRNA sets the order of amino acids in the peptide.
checklist: Says the ribosome reads the mRNA 5′ to 3′ in codons of three bases, starting at the start codon AUG
Says each tRNA anticodon pairs with a complementary codon, so the codon picks which tRNA, and so which amino acid, comes next (for example anticodon 3′ CGA 5′ pairs with GCU and brings Ala)
Says the ribosome joins each new amino acid to the chain with a peptide bond, then moves one codon along
Says no tRNA pairs with the stop codon UAA, so translation ends and the four-amino-acid peptide is released

earns.answer: The ribosome reads the mRNA from 5′ to 3′, three bases at a time, starting at the start codon AUG. Each codon pairs with a tRNA whose anticodon is complementary to it. AUG pairs with the tRNA carrying Met. The next codon, GCU, pairs with the anticodon 3′ CGA 5′, and that tRNA carries Ala. The ribosome forms a peptide bond between Met and Ala, then moves along one codon. UGG brings Trp and AAA brings Lys in the same way. No tRNA pairs with UAA, a stop codon, so a release factor ends translation and the peptide Met-Ala-Trp-Lys is released. The order of codons sets the order of amino acids.
earns.why: It walks through the model step by step: reading frame, codon and anticodon pairing, bond formation and the stop, with a worked example.

misses.answer: The mRNA codons code for amino acids, so the ribosome puts them in order using the genetic code.
misses.why: It restates the result. It never says how tRNA anticodons pair with codons or how the ribosome reads three bases at a time and stops.

prompts.title: Lactose, glucose and enzyme levels
prompts.context:
E. coli makes β-galactosidase, an enzyme that breaks lactose into glucose and galactose, from a gene in the lac operon. Researchers grew E. coli on four media and measured β-galactosidase activity. Glycerol is a carbon source that does not affect the lac operon directly.

Mediumβ-galactosidase activity (units/mg protein)
Glycerol5
Glycerol + lactose1,000
Glucose5
Glucose + lactose80
prompts.prompt: Describe the effect of lactose on β-galactosidase activity with and without glucose present, using values from the table.
checklist: Without glucose, adding lactose raises activity from 5 to 1,000 units/mg protein, a 200-fold increase
With glucose, adding lactose raises activity only from 5 to 80 units/mg protein, a 16-fold increase
Compares the two lactose media: glucose lowers activity from 1,000 to 80 units/mg protein, 92% lower
Concludes lactose turns on enzyme production, but much less when glucose is also present

earns.answer: Lactose increases β-galactosidase activity, and glucose reduces that increase. Without glucose, adding lactose raises activity from 5 to 1,000 units/mg protein, a 200-fold increase. With glucose present, adding lactose raises activity only from 5 to 80 units/mg protein, a 16-fold increase. When lactose is present, glucose lowers activity from 1,000 to 80 units/mg protein, which is 92% lower. Without lactose, activity stays at 5 units/mg protein whether or not glucose is present.
earns.why: It describes each comparison with values, units and the size and direction of the change, which is what a describe task asks for.

misses.answer: Lactose increases the enzyme and glucose decreases it.
misses.why: It gives no values or units, no size of change.

prompts.title: Two changes in the same codon
prompts.context: A gene codes for an enzyme 300 amino acids long. Codon 12 of its mRNA is GAA, which codes for glutamic acid. Two mutations are found in different individuals. In mutation A, the third base of codon 12 changes, so the codon becomes GAG, which also codes for glutamic acid. In mutation B, one extra base is inserted in codon 12.
prompts.prompt: Predict the effect of each mutation on the enzyme's function, and justify each prediction.
checklist: Predicts mutation A has no effect: GAG still codes for glutamic acid, so the amino acid sequence is unchanged
Predicts mutation B most likely makes a nonfunctional enzyme
Justifies B with a frameshift: every codon after the insertion is read in a new frame, so most amino acids after the insertion change
Adds that the new frame is likely to hit a stop codon early, giving a short protein that cannot fold into the working shape

earns.answer: Mutation A will not change the enzyme's function. GAG codes for glutamic acid, the same as GAA, so the amino acid sequence, the folding and the active site stay the same. Mutation B will most likely make the enzyme nonfunctional. The ribosome reads mRNA in groups of three bases, so one inserted base shifts the reading frame for every codon after it. Most of the amino acids from about position 12 onward will be different, and a stop codon is likely to appear early in the new frame, giving a short protein. That protein cannot fold into the enzyme's normal shape, so it cannot catalyze the reaction.
earns.why: It gives a prediction for each mutation and justifies it with how codons are read, linking sequence to folding to function.

misses.answer: Both mutations change the DNA, so both will change the enzyme and stop it from working.
misses.why: A change in DNA does not always change the protein: GAG and GAA code for the same amino acid. It gives no reason why the insertion matters.

prompts.title: Controls in a PCR food test
prompts.context:
A lab tests a cookie labeled "peanut-free" for peanut DNA. It uses PCR with primers that copy a 180 base pair section of a peanut gene, then runs the products on a gel.

LaneWhat was loadedResult
1DNA ladder of known sizesBands at 100, 200, 300 bp and up
2PCR product from cookie DNABand at 180 bp
3PCR product from pure peanut DNABand at 180 bp
4PCR with water instead of DNANo band
prompts.prompt: Explain what lane 3 and lane 4 each rule out, and justify the lab's conclusion about the cookie.
checklist: Lane 3 is a positive control: it shows the primers and the reaction work and that peanut DNA gives a 180 bp band, ruling out a failed reaction as the reason for any missing band
Lane 4 is a negative control: with no DNA added there is no band, ruling out peanut DNA contaminating the reagents as the source of the band in lane 2
Concludes the cookie contains peanut DNA, because lane 2 has a band of the same size as the peanut control, read against the ladder

earns.answer: Lane 3 is a positive control. Pure peanut DNA gives a band at 180 bp, so the primers and the PCR reagents work and the expected band size is known. This rules out a failed reaction as the reason a sample might show no band. Lane 4 is a negative control. With water in place of DNA there is no band, so the reagents are not contaminated with peanut DNA. This rules out contamination as the source of the band in lane 2. Lane 2 has a band at 180 bp, the same size as lane 3, judged against the ladder in lane 1. So the cookie contains peanut DNA, and the "peanut-free" label is not supported.
earns.why: It names each control's type and says exactly which other explanation it removes, then uses the band sizes to support the conclusion.

misses.answer: Lanes 3 and 4 are the controls. The cookie has peanut DNA because there is a band in lane 2.
misses.why: It labels the controls without saying what each one rules out, so it cannot show why the band in lane 2 can be trusted.

prompts.title: Did the insecticide cause resistance?
prompts.context:
Farmers began spraying an insecticide on a field in 2016. Researchers measured the frequency of an allele that makes beetles resistant to it. The 2016 sample was collected and frozen just before the first spraying. Beetles in this population have about one generation per year.

YearResistance allele frequency
2016 (before spraying)0.02
20180.09
20200.27
20220.48
20240.61

A student claims the insecticide caused resistance mutations in the beetles that were sprayed.
prompts.prompt: Support or refute the student's claim using evidence from the table and reasoning about natural selection.
checklist: Refutes the claim that the insecticide caused the resistance mutations
Evidence: the resistance allele was already present, at a frequency of 0.02, in beetles collected before any spraying
Evidence: the allele frequency rose to 0.61 by 2024, over about 8 generations of spraying
Reasoning: spraying killed more susceptible beetles, so resistant beetles survived and reproduced more and passed on the allele; mutations arise at random, not because they are needed

earns.answer: The data refute the claim. The resistance allele was already in the population before spraying began: beetles frozen in 2016, before the first spray, had an allele frequency of 0.02. So the insecticide did not create it. After spraying started, the frequency rose to 0.09 in 2018, 0.27 in 2020 and 0.61 in 2024. The insecticide killed more susceptible beetles than resistant ones. Resistant beetles survived and left more offspring, and those offspring inherited the allele. Over about 8 generations of this selection, the allele became more common. Mutations arise at random; the environment selects among the variation already present.
earns.why: It uses the key evidence (the allele was present before exposure) plus the trend, and explains the rise with differential survival and reproduction.

misses.answer: The claim is wrong because the beetles evolved resistance by natural selection, not by mutation.
misses.why: It names a process but cites no data, especially the 0.02 frequency before spraying, and does not explain how selection raised the frequency.

prompts.title: Is this population at equilibrium?
prompts.context: A gene in a wildflower population has two alleles, A and a. A survey of 500 plants found 245 AA, 190 Aa and 65 aa. At p = 0.05, the critical value is 3.84 for 1 degree of freedom and 5.99 for 2 degrees of freedom.
prompts.prompt: Calculate the expected genotype counts under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and a chi-square value, and determine whether the population is in equilibrium for this gene.
checklist: Allele frequencies from the counts: p = (2 × 245 + 190) ÷ 1,000 = 0.68 and q = 0.32
Expected counts: AA = p² × 500 = 231.2, Aa = 2pq × 500 = 217.6, aa = q² × 500 = 51.2
Compares with the critical value: 8.04 is larger than 3.84 and 5.99, so equilibrium is rejected, with fewer heterozygotes (190 versus 217.6) than expected

earns.answer: There are 1,000 alleles. p = (2 × 245 + 190) ÷ 1,000 = 0.68, so q = 0.32. Expected counts are AA = 0.4624 × 500 = 231.2, Aa = 0.4352 × 500 = 217.6 and aa = 0.1024 × 500 = 51.2. Chi-square = (245 − 231.2)²/231.2 + (190 − 217.6)²/217.6 + (65 − 51.2)²/51.2 = 0.824 + 3.501 + 3.720 ≈ 8.04. This is larger than the critical value with either 1 or 2 degrees of freedom, so I reject the null hypothesis: the population is not in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for this gene. It has fewer heterozygotes than expected (190 versus 217.6) and more of both homozygotes.
earns.why: It computes allele frequencies from the observed genotypes, shows expected counts and the test, rejects the null correctly and describes the direction of the departure.

misses.answer: The population is not in equilibrium because the genotypes are not in a 1:2:1 ratio.
misses.why: Hardy-Weinberg expected counts come from p² : 2pq : q², not 1:2:1, and no chi-square test is done to judge the size of the difference.

prompts.title: Reading relatedness from a tree
prompts.context:
A phylogenetic tree of four beetle species, W, X, Y and Z, built from DNA sequences, shows this branching order: Z splits off first from the common ancestor of all four. Next, W splits from the lineage leading to X and Y. Last, X and Y split from each other. Species Z, W and X all have hind wings; species Y has none.

A student claims that X is more closely related to W than to Y, because X and W both have hind wings.
prompts.prompt: Use the tree to evaluate the student's claim.
checklist: Says relatedness is read from the most recent common ancestor (the branch points), not from shared traits
Says X and Y share a common ancestor that W does not share, so X is more closely related to Y; the claim is wrong
Explains the shared wings: hind wings are also in Z, so they were most likely present in the common ancestor of all four and lost in the lineage leading to Y

earns.answer: The claim is wrong. On a tree, how closely two species are related depends on how recently they shared a common ancestor. X and Y split from each other last, so they share a common ancestor that W does not. X is therefore more closely related to Y than to W. Shared hind wings do not show close relationship here. Z, which split off first, also has hind wings, so hind wings were most likely present in the common ancestor of all four species. W and X kept this ancestral trait, and hind wings were lost in the lineage leading to Y after it split from X.
earns.why: It uses the branch points of the tree to judge relatedness and explains the trait pattern with the tree instead of letting the trait decide.

misses.answer: The claim is wrong because the tree is based on DNA, and DNA is more accurate than traits like wings.
misses.why: It does not read the tree: no most recent common ancestor, no explanation of why W and X share wings while Y lacks them.

prompts.title: From a barrier to separate species
prompts.context: A tree frog population was split by a mountain ridge that formed about a million years ago. Today, males on the east side call at about 32 pulses per second and males on the west side at about 51 pulses per second. In playback trials, east-side females moved toward the east-side call in 18 of 20 trials, and west-side females moved toward the west-side call in 17 of 20 trials. In a small area where the two groups now meet, almost no hybrids are found.
prompts.prompt: Explain how the separation by the ridge could have led to reproductive isolation between the two groups of frogs.
checklist: Says the ridge blocked gene flow between the two populations
Says each population changed independently: different mutations arose, and natural selection and genetic drift changed allele frequencies differently on each side
Links the divergence to the different calls (32 versus 51 pulses per second) and to females preferring their own population's call
Names behavioral isolation, a prezygotic barrier, that keeps the groups from interbreeding even where they meet

earns.answer: The ridge blocked gene flow, so alleles could no longer move between the east and west populations. Each population then changed on its own. Different mutations arose on each side, natural selection acted on them under different conditions, and genetic drift changed allele frequencies at random. Over about a million years, genes that affect calling and call preference diverged. East-side males now call at about 32 pulses per second and west-side males at about 51, and females chose their own population's call in 18 of 20 trials (east) and 17 of 20 trials (west). Because females respond mostly to their own population's call, the groups rarely mate even where they meet. This behavioral isolation is a prezygotic barrier, so the two groups are now reproductively isolated.
earns.why: It gives the full chain: no gene flow, independent change by mutation, selection and drift, then a behavioral barrier, tied to the data.

misses.answer: The ridge separated the frogs, so they became different species with different calls.
misses.why: It restates the outcome. It does not say that gene flow stopped, what made the populations diverge or how the calls block interbreeding.

prompts.title: Where the other 90% goes
prompts.context: In a grassland food chain, energy stored in new biomass each year is: producers 20,000 kcal/m², primary consumers 2,000 kcal/m², secondary consumers 200 kcal/m² and tertiary consumers 20 kcal/m².
prompts.prompt: Explain why only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is stored as biomass at the next level, and what this means for the number of trophic levels the grassland can support.
checklist: Says most of the energy an organism takes in is used in cellular respiration and leaves the ecosystem as heat
Says some energy is never eaten or absorbed: uneaten plant parts, feces and dead bodies pass to decomposers instead
Says only the energy stored in new biomass is available to the next trophic level
Concludes that energy shrinks tenfold at each step (20,000 to 20 kcal/m² in three steps), so too little remains to support more than a few levels

earns.answer: Primary consumers do not eat all of the producers' biomass, and of what they eat, some is not digested and leaves as feces. That energy goes to decomposers, not to the next level. Of the energy consumers do absorb, most is used in cellular respiration to power movement, active transport and the building of molecules, and that energy leaves as heat. Only the energy stored in new biomass, about 10%, can be eaten by the next level. So energy falls tenfold at each step, from 20,000 to 2,000 to 200 to 20 kcal/m². After a few steps too little energy is left to support another population, so food chains have only a few trophic levels.
earns.why: It accounts for where the missing energy goes (not eaten, not absorbed, lost as heat in respiration) and uses the data to explain the limit on trophic levels.

misses.answer: Each level only gets 10% of the energy because the rest is lost, so there are not many trophic levels.
misses.why: It restates the 10% figure. It never says how the energy is lost: respiration, heat and material that is never eaten or absorbed.

prompts.title: Growth of a Paramecium culture
prompts.context:
A student added Paramecium to a flask of culture medium and counted them every 2 days. Fresh food was added every 2 days at the same rate.

DayDensity (cells/mL)

prompts.prompt: Describe the pattern of population growth, using values from the table, and identify the carrying capacity.
checklist: Growth starts slowly, from 10 to 40 cells/mL over days 0 to 2 (15 cells/mL per day)
Growth is fastest between days 4 and 6: from 150 to 380 cells/mL, about 115 cells/mL per day
Growth slows and levels off: from 560 to 570 cells/mL over days 10 to 12, only 5 cells/mL per day
Identifies the carrying capacity as about 570 cells/mL and names the pattern as logistic growth

earns.answer: The population shows logistic growth. It grows slowly at first, from 10 to 40 cells/mL over days 0 to 2, a rate of 15 cells/mL per day. Growth is fastest between days 4 and 6, when density rises from 150 to 380 cells/mL, about 115 cells/mL per day. After that the rate falls: 70 cells/mL per day between days 6 and 8, and only 5 cells/mL per day between days 10 and 12, when density goes from 560 to 570 cells/mL. The population levels off at a carrying capacity of about 570 cells/mL, where the food supply and the buildup of wastes limit further growth.
earns.why: It describes each phase with values, units and rates, names the pattern and reads the carrying capacity from where the curve levels off.

misses.answer: The population grew quickly and then stopped growing at its carrying capacity.
misses.why: It gives no values, rates or units and does not state the carrying capacity as a number.

prompts.title: A removal experiment with cages
prompts.context: Two snail species, A and B, graze algae on intertidal rocks. Ecologists placed mesh cages over 20 rock patches. In 10 cages they removed all species A snails; in the other 10 they left both species. At the start, species B density was 40 snails/m² in both groups. After one year it was 95 snails/m² in the removal cages and 42 snails/m² in the cages with both species.
prompts.prompt: Identify the independent and dependent variables, explain what the cages with both species rule out, and state what the results suggest about how A and B interact.
checklist: Independent variable: whether species A is present (removed or left in the cage)
Dependent variable: density of species B, in snails/m², after one year
Says the cages with both species have the same cages, rocks and year, ruling out the cages themselves or changes in weather or algae over the year as the cause of the rise in B
Concludes the rise from 40 to 95 snails/m² happened only when A was removed, which is evidence that A competes with B

earns.answer: The independent variable is whether species A is present: removed or left in the cage. The dependent variable is the density of species B in snails/m² after one year. The cages with both species are the control. They had the same mesh cages, the same kind of rocks and the same year as the removal cages. In them, B changed only from 40 to 42 snails/m². This rules out the cages themselves, or changes in weather or algae growth during the year, as the reason B increased. B rose to 95 snails/m² only where A was removed, so A was holding B down, which is evidence of competition between the two species for algae.
earns.why: It names the variables with units, says exactly which other causes the control cages remove and draws the conclusion the comparison allows.

misses.answer: The independent variable is species A and the dependent variable is species B. The cages with both species are the control group.
misses.why: The variables are vague (no presence or absence, no density or units), and it labels the control without saying what it rules out.

prompts.title: More species, less diversity?
prompts.context:
Ecologists counted the first 100 plants along the same transect in a meadow before and five years after an invasive plant arrived. Simpson's diversity index is D = 1 − Σ(n/N)².

SpeciesBefore (plants)After (plants)
Native 13010
Native 2258
Native 3257
Native 4205
Invasive plant070

A student claims the invasive plant made the meadow more diverse, because the number of species rose from 4 to 5.
prompts.prompt: Support or refute the student's claim using Simpson's diversity index and reasoning about what diversity measures.
checklist: Refutes the claim that the meadow became more diverse
Calculates D before ≈ 0.75 (1 − 0.255) and D after ≈ 0.49 (1 − 0.514)
Reasons that diversity depends on evenness as well as the number of species: one species now makes up 70 of 100 plants
Notes the native plants fell from 100 to 30, so the community is dominated by one species

earns.answer: The data refute the claim. Before the invasion, D = 1 − (0.30² + 0.25² + 0.25² + 0.20²) = 1 − 0.255 ≈ 0.75. After it, D = 1 − (0.70² + 0.10² + 0.08² + 0.07² + 0.05²) = 1 − 0.514 ≈ 0.49. Diversity fell even though species richness rose from 4 to 5. Simpson's index measures how evenly individuals are spread among species as well as how many species there are. Before, the four natives were close to equal in number. After, the invasive plant makes up 70 of 100 plants and the natives dropped from 100 plants to 30, so two plants picked at random are much more likely to be the same species.
earns.why: It calculates the index before and after, uses the drop as evidence and explains why evenness, not just species count, sets diversity.

misses.answer: The claim is wrong because the invasive plant took over, so the meadow is less diverse.
misses.why: It gives no index values and no reasoning about evenness, so it does not show why one more species can still mean lower diversity.
